title: Goblin Tumble and the Peculiar Treasure
markdown:
The Whispering Mountains looked like giant grumpy teeth trying to chomp the sky. The wind did not just whistle. It sang opera, told ghost stories, and sometimes, if you listened closely, complained about the neighbours. It was enough to make knees go wobbly like overcooked jelly. Tiny observatories perched like bird nests on the tips of peaks, snooping at glittering stars. Tumble lived up there, ears humming whenever a zany idea buzzed in his noggin. Pickle rode his shoulder: less a pet than a furry advisor with a nose for trouble and, of course, cheese. His whiskers twitched with more wisdom than most wizards.

On a particularly Tuesdayish afternoon—the kind of day that feels like a Monday wearing a mismatched hat and still hasn’t had its morning yawn—Tumble’s coin pouch proved as empty as a ghost’s lunchbox. A few forgotten pebbles. No clink. His tummy staged a rebellion of a thousand hungry grubs throwing a noisy party. Admitting he was as broke as a broken bauble? Never. Tumble was far too Tumble-ish for that.

“Operation: Magnificent Meal is a GO,” he declared, puffing until his patched tunic strained, nearly knocking Pickle off his perch. Pickle, sleek, eyes like polished obsidian, gave a tiny sigh. He had heard this preamble. It usually meant peculiar clues and a lot of optimistic grunting.

The map had belonged to Great-Uncle Gribble, a goblin of questionable sanity, spectacular mismatched socks, and an uncanny gift for getting lost in his own kitchen. Smudges like dried berry juice. Scribbles that might have been bird droppings or codes. A smell of burnt toast and lingering regret. It promised the Glimmering Hoard of the High Peaks, which sounded expensive enough for several suppers and maybe a new hat.

“Three paces east of the sighing stone, beneath the eye that never blinks.”

“A sighing stone?” Pickle’s whiskers twitched. “Does it require a therapist, or just a good breeze?”

“Precisely. Technically correct. Emotional helpfulness is… interpretive.”

Interpretive was a very polite word for utterly baffling. They trekked for ages, scrambling over rocks, ducking under ancient gnarled branches that looked like skeletal fingers. They found a stone, yes: grey, lump-shaped, profoundly bored. When the wind, feeling whimsical, blew through a tiny whispering crack, it made a sound remarkably like a weary sigh. So far, so good. Pickle even gave it a little nod. But the eye that never blinks? A puzzle worthy of a thousand Gribble-coins.

They searched high and low. Tumble peered into knotholes that seemed to wink, squinted at shimmering mica that danced in sunlight, even suspected a round moss-covered mushroom with a curious unblinking spot. He asked a grumpy-looking beetle, who scuttled away muttering about impudent goblins.

Crisis two: “Aha. The eye. It’s a puddle.”

A small perfect puddle, reflecting indifferent sky. It did not blink. Tumble dug with the frantic energy of a badger after an extra-juicy worm. Sore fingers. Mud from brow to chin, a miniature swamp monster. He found a single tarnished button.

“Not even a shiny one. This map is utter rubbish. A Gribble-disappointment.”

“Or,” Pickle murmured, nudging the button, “it’s very specific about what it doesn’t contain.”

Tumble scowled. His tummy began an angry opera. Then a thought, bright as a polished acorn: dusty observatories, brass telescopes, a leaning shop sign, The Celestial Curio Shop – Peculiarities for the Perplexed. What was more peculiar than a map that led to a button and a puddle?

“We’re going to trade.”

They scrambled down squiggly mule paths, button scooped, puddle cupped in a sturdy leaf. The descent was faster than the climb, which was typical of goblins who had just invented a new kind of treasure. Dawn painted the east rosy. A misty tendril curled around a distant bell tower. The tower, still sleepy, chimed one resonant note. Tumble stopped. Pickle’s whiskers stilled. For a moment the mountain was only colour and that single bell, and nobody needed coins. Then Tumble’s tummy composed a smaller, more polite opera, and they hurried on.

The shop leaned as if it had had one too many star-gazing sessions. Inside: shimmering stardust, bottled whispers, a petrified sneeze. Professor Sprout, spectacles on the tip of his nose (not that Professor Sprout, a different one, equally fond of gardening and peculiar ingredients), polished a crystal ball of captured moonlight.

“A unique item for trade.” Tumble presented the button, trying to sound like a goblin who regularly dealt in mystical artifacts.

“A genuine Gribble-Button. Quite rare. Each holds the echo of a goblin’s boast.” Sprout peered at the leaf. “And a Whisper-Mountain Dewdrop, caught at the dawn sigh. Fascinating moisture. A hint of mountain melancholy.”

“So you’ll give me coins?”

Sprout chuckled, tiny bells. “Not a shopping list with ambition. Artifacts. A story. The button for a discerning waistcoat at the sock-swapping convention. The dewdrop for an anxious pixie’s garden. For these: one rather hefty coin pouch.”

CLINK-CLANK-CLUNK. The symphony of a well-fed goblin. Tumble practically vibrated. They exchanged peculiarities for supper-securing weight.

“The map wasn’t wrong. It was misunderstood. Great-Uncle Gribble was a genius. A sock-loving, treasure-finding genius.”

Pickle chirped and nuzzled an ear. He had known Tumble would figure it out. He always did, eventually, after a certain amount of mud. That night Tumble and Pickle enjoyed the most magnificent supper of roasted roots that tasted like sunshine, plump juicy grubs that popped with flavour (and no one dared call them gross), and a generous slice of berry crumble. Pickle got an extra grub. Naturally. Even a pragmatic rat deserves a reward for putting up with a goblin’s grand ideas. The pouch sat on the table and made no speeches about cleverness. The sighing stone, far up the tooth of the mountain, sighed once more, probably from habit, and Tumble, for once, let it.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
